title: Game Day Results — Hosted Overload Protection (Circuit Breakers + Load Shedding)
content:
Doc: Post-game-day notes for Hosted circuit breakers + load shedding
Owner: Rafael Mendes (SRE)
Date executed: 2025-12-16
Region: us-east (canary stack)
Primary models under test: rwd-llama-70b-instruct (chat), rwd-qwen-32b (chat), embeddings route (small)

Attendees (primary):
- SRE: Rafael Mendes, Christine Wong, Tomáš Novák
- Platform/Routing: Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon, Elena Popov
- Gateway: Amara Diallo
- Runtime: Noah Patel, Lena Fischer, Samir Qureshi
- Observability: Aisha Bello, Sergio Costa
- Release coord: Connor O’Brien

Purpose
Validate end-to-end overload protection behavior (edge → routing/control plane → runtime/GPU pools) under controlled traffic spikes and degraded capacity.
Success criteria (high-level):
1) No cascading failure (control plane stays responsive; no runaway queue growth).
2) Deterministic, documented customer-facing errors (stable 429/503 + Redwood error codes + Retry-After).
3) Breakers do not flap; recovery is predictable.
4) Dashboards/alerts are actionable and do not page for expected load shedding.

What we tested (scenarios)
S1. Step-function traffic spike (non-streaming chat)
- Ramp: baseline 500 RPS → 4,000 RPS within 30s, sustain 10 min.
- Expectation: early shed begins before GPU pool saturation causes tail-latency collapse; breaker opens per (model, region, tier).

S2. Long-prompt spike + high max_tokens (chat)
- Mixed: 30% of traffic with 12–18k prompt tokens, max_tokens 1–2k.
- Expectation: prefill pressure triggers shed signals earlier; bounded queues prevent prefill backlog from starving small requests.

S3. Streaming stress (chat streaming)
- High concurrency streaming, simulate client disconnects + retries.
- Expectation: streaming disconnects do not amplify load; shed reasons are consistent; guidance is not “retry immediately”.

S4. Capacity brownout simulation
- Artificially drain 35–45% of GPU pool capacity in us-east for rwd-llama-70b-instruct.
- Expectation: breaker opens quickly; routing fallback policy only triggers when configured; control plane not overloaded by retry storms.

S5. Control plane latency injection
- Inject 200–400ms additional latency to routing service (breaker evaluation API) for 5 min.
- Expectation: gateway admission control sheds early and does not pile up; routing remains stable; timeouts produce correct mapping.

S6. KV-cache / memory pressure
- Force conditions that increase KV-cache churn (sequence-length distribution shift + concurrency).
- Expectation: runtime guardrail sheds before OOM/thrash; clear reason code is propagated.


Observed metrics (highlights)
NOTE: Numbers below are from the canary stack only, not production fleet-wide. These are directional for behavior validation.

Across scenarios (general):
- Control plane availability: no 5xx surge from routing service itself; p99 for breaker evaluation API stayed < 180ms except during S5 injection where it reached ~520ms p99 (expected).
- Gateway response semantics: 429 and 503 were stable, with Retry-After present for overload-shed responses.
- Runtime queue depth: bounded queues prevented unbounded growth; we saw queue depth clamp at configured limits and corresponding shed.

S1 (Step spike):
- Prior baseline behavior (pre-game-day reference): p99 latency frequently exceeded 12–20s and timeouts cascaded, with mixed 502/503.
- With overload protection:
  - p99 latency peaked at ~2.8s for successful responses during the initial ramp, then stabilized ~1.3–1.7s during sustained load.
  - Shed rate (gateway + runtime combined): peaked ~41% during minute 2–4, settled ~22–28% during sustained spike.
  - Response code mix during peak: 429 ~31%, 503 ~10%, internal 5xx < 0.3%.
  - Breaker transitions: closed → open within ~18–35s after ramp start for the hottest route; half-open attempts began ~120s after load reduction.

S2 (Long prompts):
- Prefill scheduling became the dominant bottleneck.
- Observed: small requests were still served with acceptable latency when shed was enabled; without shed (feature flag off in a short A/B window), small requests’ p99 degraded rapidly.
- Runtime shed reason distribution (approx):
  - RUNTIME_QUEUE_FULL: ~52%
  - RUNTIME_PREFILL_PRESSURE: ~33%
  - ROUTING_BREAKER_OPEN (received downstream hint): ~11%
  - OTHER: ~4%
- Key win: bounded queues + prefill-pressure shed prevented the “tail latency spiral” we’ve seen in real incidents.

S3 (Streaming):
- We reproduced a failure mode where a synthetic client retried aggressively on stream disconnect and amplified shed rate.
- With correct client behavior (exponential backoff + jitter), shed rate reduced materially and breaker recovered faster.
- Observed streaming-specific issues:
  - Some disconnects were mapped to generic “upstream connection closed” in logs instead of overload reason codes (gap in gateway logging context propagation).

S4 (Brownout):
- Routing breaker opened correctly for affected (model, region, tier).
- Fallback behavior:
  - Fallback to alternate region worked when enabled, but we found two cases of “fallback bounce” (region A→B→A) when both regions were partially constrained and customer policy was permissive.
  - Policy guardrails blocked one unsafe config (good), but did not block the bounce loop pattern (needs enhancement).
- Customer-visible semantics were consistent: 503 with overload code + Retry-After (when no safe fallback).

S5 (Control plane latency injection):
- Expected increase in admission shedding at the edge to keep routing from becoming the bottleneck.
- Issue found: gateway’s timeout to routing breaker API was set too aggressively for the injected latency; this caused a short window of generic 503 without Redwood overload code.
- Once timeout increased (manual config), error mapping became consistent.

S6 (KV-cache / memory pressure):
- Runtime shed-before-OOM worked; no OOMs observed.
- Metric correlation looked good: KV-cache pressure metric rose, then shed, then pressure stabilized.
- One gap: sampling on high-cardinality labels caused delayed ingestion in one dashboard panel (see Observability findings).


What worked (wins)
1) Layering worked: shedding early at gateway + bounded runtime queues prevented cascading failures.
2) Breaker hysteresis mostly behaved: we didn’t see rapid open/close oscillation in normal spikes.
3) Customer-facing error semantics were substantially clearer than baseline:
   - 429 used primarily for admission shedding.
   - 503 used primarily for capacity constrained / breaker open (when admission didn’t catch it earlier).
   - Retry-After present and generally aligned with recovery times (see tuning items).
4) Dashboards were usable in real time:
   - Breaker state by (model, tier) and shed reason breakdown were the most actionable panels.
   - Queue depth clamp visualization helped confirm runtime protection was engaged.
5) Oncall workflow improved with runbook checklist; operators could identify “expected shed” vs “incident” faster.


What failed / issues found
P0 (must fix before broader rollout)
- P0-1: Error mapping gaps when routing breaker API times out (S5).
  - Symptom: some requests returned generic 503 without Redwood overload code; missing consistent body shape.
  - Likely cause: gateway timeout path bypasses overload error builder.
  - Impact: breaks “clear and consistent customer-actionable errors” goal.

- P0-2: Fallback bounce loop possible under partial constraints (S4).
  - Symptom: repeated routing attempts across regions for the same request class when both regions are degraded.
  - Impact: increases control plane load and delays deterministic response; can create retry-like amplification internally.

P1 (fix soon / before GA)
- P1-1: Retry-After tuning: values too low for certain recovery modes.
  - Observed: during brownout + recovery, actual stable recovery took ~90–140s; Retry-After was frequently 15–30s.
  - Impact: encourages clients to retry too quickly; increases shed and slows recovery.

- P1-2: Streaming disconnect classification incomplete.
  - Observed: some streaming terminations not tagged with overload reason in logs/traces.
  - Impact: support/oncall can’t reliably explain customer’s disconnect vs overload.

- P1-3: Breaker half-open test traffic not sufficiently bounded.
  - Observed: half-open allowed a burst larger than intended (configuration ambiguity). Didn’t cause incident, but it’s too risky.

P2 (polish)
- P2-1: Metric label cardinality in one panel (route/model + customer_id) caused ingestion lag during high load.
  - Root: accidental inclusion of a high-cardinality label in a debug metric.
  - Impact: delayed visibility during the most important moments.

- P2-2: Alert noise: one alert fired for elevated 429 rate even though it was an expected shed scenario.
  - Impact: paging risk unless rule is aligned with “overload-protected errors are not internal failures”.


Customer impact assessment (simulated)
- For well-behaved clients, the new behavior is a clear improvement: faster failures with explicit instructions (Retry-After) and fewer ambiguous timeouts.
- For poorly-behaved clients (no jitter / immediate retry), overload protection prevents platform collapse but still results in prolonged client-visible errors. We should proactively document this and ensure SDK helpers default to jittered exponential backoff.


Key graphs/panels referenced (during game day)
- Breaker state timeline by (model, tier, region)
- Admission decision rate (allowed vs shed) at gateway
- Shed reason breakdown at runtime
- Runtime queue depth and clamp count
- GPU pool saturation proxy (utilization + queue time)
- p95/p99 latency (success only) + latency including errors
- 429/503 split with Redwood overload codes
- Control plane p99 latency (routing eval) and timeout rate


Decisions made during game day
- Keep canary enabled for us-east rwd-qwen-32b (lower-risk) while P0 items are addressed for rwd-llama-70b-instruct.
- Temporarily increase gateway timeout to routing eval API in canary to reduce generic 503 timeouts while we implement the correct error mapping path.
- Freeze changes to breaker threshold defaults until we finish Retry-After + half-open bounding tuning (avoid moving targets).


Follow-up action items
P0
1) Fix gateway timeout path to return standardized overload error payload + Redwood code
   - Owner: Amara Diallo
   - Support: Brian Murphy
   - Target: 2025-12-22
   - Notes: ensure OpenAI-compat endpoints map correctly; include Retry-After when shed is due to control-plane overload protection.

2) Add policy guardrail to prevent fallback bounce loops (A→B→A) under partial constraints
   - Owner: Jordan Lee
   - Support: Elena Popov
   - Target: 2025-12-27
   - Notes: must be deterministic; stop after N attempts and return overload-protected error; consider per-request routing context to avoid loops.

P1
3) Retry-After tuning pass (align to observed recovery time distributions)
   - Owner: Christine Wong
   - Support: Tomáš Novák
   - Target: 2025-12-30
   - Notes: incorporate cool-down/hysteresis state; consider different Retry-After for admission shed vs breaker open vs runtime pressure.

4) Bound half-open test volume explicitly (config + enforcement)
   - Owner: Ravi Menon
   - Support: Mina Haddad
   - Target: 2026-01-03
   - Notes: ensure half-open cannot exceed small fixed % of baseline capacity; verify with perf-canary scenario.

5) Streaming disconnect observability improvements (propagate overload reasons into stream termination logs/traces)
   - Owner: Noah Patel
   - Support: Omar El-Sayed
   - Target: 2026-01-05

6) Update SDK examples/tests to emphasize exponential backoff with jitter and honoring Retry-After
   - Owner: Ibrahim Khan
   - Support: Monica Patel
   - Target: 2026-01-10
   - Notes: add a regression test for “no immediate retry loop” in our sample clients.

P2
7) Remove high-cardinality metric label; re-run cardinality review
   - Owner: Allison Grant
   - Support: Caleb Johnson
   - Target: 2025-12-23

8) Alert rule adjustments: do not page on expected overload-protected error rates; page on internal failures + control plane degradation
   - Owner: Aisha Bello
   - Support: Sergio Costa
   - Target: 2025-12-29

9) Runbook updates based on game day findings
   - Owner: Owen Phillips
   - Support: Dev Patel
   - Target: 2026-01-06
   - Notes: add explicit “routing eval timeout” diagnosis path; add guidance for identifying fallback bounce symptoms.


Open questions
- Should we treat routing eval timeouts as 503 (service unavailable) or 429 (admission shed) when we intentionally shed to protect routing? (Leaning: 503 with explicit Redwood code; include Retry-After.)
- Do we need a separate overload code for “CONTROL_PLANE_PROTECTION” vs “ROUTING_BREAKER_OPEN” to reduce ambiguity?
- What is the correct default Retry-After for streaming endpoints (given streams can hold connections longer and recovery can be slower)?


Appendix: quick notes / timeline (operator log)
- T+00:00 start S1 ramp; breaker transitions begin ~T+00:25
- T+02:00 shed peaks; queue clamp counters increase; success p99 remains < 3s
- T+10:00 stop ramp; breaker half-open begins ~T+12:00; recovery observed by ~T+14:30
- T+20:00 start S4 brownout; bounce loop observed ~T+22:00 for permissive fallback policy
- T+35:00 start S5 control plane latency injection; generic 503 observed ~T+36:30; timeout config hotfix applied ~T+38:00
- T+48:00 start S6 memory pressure; shed engages; KV pressure stabilizes; no OOM

Summary
The system met the primary objective: prevent cascading failures and tail-latency collapse under overload, while returning mostly consistent customer-actionable errors. The remaining work is focused on closing P0 gaps (timeout-path error mapping and fallback bounce prevention) and tuning Retry-After/half-open behavior to reduce retry amplification and speed recovery. Dashboards are close; we need one more pass on metric cardinality and paging semantics so that expected shedding does not page as a hard incident.
